items.title: CPU-ARC: Agentic Reasoning Caching for on-CPU Reasoning Reuse
items.review_scope: Personally reread cited official fulltext paragraphs, verified cached bytes, and bound conservative bilingual summaries to those passages. Reused saved identity/date and primary/independent scope evidence. No whole-paper numerical recalculation or experimental rerun.

summary_source_claims.paragraph: A semantic function is an executable abstraction representing one logical step of the source reasoning trace, designed to be maximally reusable across semantically equivalent contexts. They are the matter of which agentic reasoning caching is made up. In our implementation, it is simply a Python callable that takes a Context object and returns a dictionary mapping natural-language descriptions to values:

ℬ \mathcal{B} enters an agentic loop in which it iteratively writes candidate semantic functions. A function remains a candidate until it passes all checks and is registered in the cache. It may be rewritten multiple times before it reaches that point.

For each candidate function, ℬ \mathcal{B} first searches the existing registry for semantically equivalent functions and inspects their source code to assess whether they can be reused directly or adapted. It then writes the candidate function body using the runtime primitives described in Section 2.1 . The candidate is validated syntactically and via static analysis of narration quality, checking that narration calls are present and that their number is commensurate with the function’s control-flow complexity. ℬ \mathcal{B} then tests the candidate by dispatching it with the original parameters and comparing its output against the corresponding fragment of the transcript, validated by a judge 𝒥 \mathcal{J} . On success, the function is registered in the cache. On failure, ℬ \mathcal{B} receives structured feedback (error messages, judge critiques, stack traces) and rewrites the candidate accordingly.

System-level caching (SLC) methods aim to address such inefficiencies by recognizing repetitive patterns in LM conversations and caching them at the level of the serving system as a whole rather than within any single inference instance. Maintained at the system level, an SLC’s entries are shared across all of the system’s inference instances and remain reusable beyond the instance in which they were born. SLC methods usually bring one or more of the following benefits:

To explore how much further the target model can be shrunk, we conducted a fine-tuning experiment. We collected 20% of the real usage examples from our benchmark evaluations, used 𝒮 \mathcal{S} to produce a synthetic training set roughly ten times larger, and finetuned Llama 3.2 1B [ 8 ] on the resulting data. The finetuned 1B-parameter model proved sufficient for the target role, and we began using it as 𝒯 \mathcal{T} in subsequent runs. Appendix D describes the data collection, synthetic augmentation, and training procedure in detail.

All costs in Table 2 use March 2026 API rates for cost accounting. The source and builder models (Claude Opus 4.5) are priced at $5.00/M input tokens, $25.00/M output tokens, $6.25/M cache-write tokens, and $0.50/M cache-read tokens. The builder’s multi-turn implementation loop is prompt-cached, so the majority of its input tokens are served from cache at the cache-read rate, significantly reducing builder costs relative to a naïve implementation without caching. For cost accounting, calls to the finetuned Llama 3.2 1B model in the target, extractor, and converter roles are valued at $0.023/M input tokens and $0.194/M output tokens, with no prompt-cache discount. The “cache cost” column is the sum of target, extractor, and converter costs incurred at invocation time.

We note that builder costs range from 12 × 12\times to 84 × 84\times the source invocation cost. This multiplier is characteristically lower for difficult problems where the source model’s reasoning is long but the resulting computation is straightforward to execute (e.g. 12 12 – 13 × 13\times for AIME), and higher for simpler problems where the source model responds briefly but the cache still requires full construction (e.g. 84 × 84\times for GSM8K). Conversely, the savings multiplier at invocation time ranges from 16 × 16\times to 291 × 291\times , with considerably higher savings on difficult competition mathematics (AIME: 262 262 – 291 × 291\times ) where the source model’s per-query cost is highest. Even on simple benchmarks such as GSM8K, the cache delivers a 16 × 16\times cost reduction per invocation. In absolute terms, cache invocation costs are uniformly low across all benchmarks ($0.0004–$0.0019 per sample), owing to the use of a small finetuned open-source target model. Let B B denote the one-time builder cost, S S the source cost per query, and C C the cache cost per invocation. For S > C S>C , the break-even point is B / ( S − C ) B/(S-C) invocations, rounded up to the next whole invocation; the Build × \times multiplier B / S B/S approximates this when C C is negligible relative to S S . Using the reported cost multipliers, ARCs for AIME problems pay for themselves after approximately 13 neighbourhood invocations, while GSM8K requires approximately 90.

summary_override.summary_en: CPU-ARC turns reasoning steps into reusable Python semantic functions. Its builder revises candidates using execution errors, judge feedback, and checks, then registers successful functions in a system-level cache for later inference. The qualifying mechanism is feedback-driven revision of executable components. Separate small-model finetuning experiments mean the whole paper should not be described as weight-frozen, and inference savings alone do not establish net savings after construction costs.

items.title: From LoRA to Language: Recovering Skill Documents from Adapters
items.review_scope: Personally reread cited official fulltext paragraphs, verified cached bytes, and bound conservative bilingual summaries to those passages. Reused saved identity/date and primary/independent scope evidence. No whole-paper numerical recalculation or experimental rerun.

summary_source_claims.paragraph: In the main one-session arm the agent never sees a reward: its score is how often the base model with its draft picks the same action as the adapted model at about 500 500 development states, so anything it learns about the task it learns from the adapter. In the reward loop , the writer instead sees task success on 60 60 development games, revises its drafts over up to five rounds, and the final round is chosen on 80 80 further development games that the writer never sees; the test games are played once per final skill. A linter rejects drafts that name specific objects (“drawer 2”), copy long passages or exceed 800 800 words. An audit of the test wins, described in Appendix G.1 , found no exploits.

A skill document and a LoRA can carry the same behaviour, but they are not equally useful. A document can be read and reviewed like code, edited in one line, combined with other skills, and given unchanged to a different model or agent harness. A LoRA is tied to the weights and tokenizer of the base model it was trained on: it does not load on Llama if it was trained on Qwen, nor on a model served only through an API, and changing one rule means retraining it. Recovering the document turns a model-locked artefact back into a portable one. We therefore measure recovery in two ways: the share of the original’s instructions that the recovered document states, and the share of the original’s task gain that it restores.

Agent skills are short documents that teach a language model how to handle a class of tasks. To save context, these documents are increasingly compiled into low-rank adapters (LoRA), which keep the behaviour but lose the text: an adapter is hard to read, edit, audit or move to another model. We ask whether the skill document can be written back from the adapter and its frozen base model, and we score each recovered document by the share of the original’s key instructions it states and by the tasks it solves. Reading the weights alone recovered little with the methods we tried; a learned map from weights to text passed on about one bit of the document. Running the adapter worked much better. The Executing Writer , a small writer trained on top of the adapted model, recovers 39 39 – 44 % 44\% of the key instructions of held-out skills, against 1.3 1.3 – 1.5 % 1.5\% with another skill’s adapter, and on adapters fitted to 41 41 external skills its documents restore 85 85 – 91 % 91\% of the original’s task gain. These strongest results are on adapters whose training stored the document; adapters trained on behaviour alone are much harder for trained writers ( 1 1 – 2 % 2\% of instructions). For these adapters we test an agent that runs the base and adapted models and writes a skill from where they differ. On ALFWorld its skills recover 58 58 – 71 % 71\% of a LoRA’s gain and carry over to models that cannot load the LoRA, lifting Llama-3.1-8B from 5 % 5\% to 55 % 55\% . Whether such a skill comes from the adapter depends on what the adapter learned: when its behaviour cannot be guessed, the adapter is the source; when it can, a reward loop without the adapter does as well.

summary_override.summary_zh: From LoRA to Language 中与本专题直接相关的是技能文档的奖励循环：writer 根据开发任务的成功反馈逐轮修订草稿，再用未见的开发游戏选择版本，最终测试另行进行。技能文档可交给执行模型复用。收录仅针对这条反馈修订技能的分支，不把适配器恢复或 writer 训练本身当作 Harness 演化，也不把全部收益归因于读取 LoRA。
summary_override.summary_en: The Harness-relevant branch of From LoRA to Language is its reward loop for skill documents. A writer revises drafts across rounds using development-task success feedback, selects a version on unseen development games, and is evaluated separately on final tests. The document can be reused by an executing model. Inclusion is limited to feedback-driven skill revision; adapter recovery and writer training alone are not Harness evolution, and the gains should not all be attributed to reading LoRA.

items.title: AutoRefine: Auto-Calibrating Code Judges from Workflow Outcomes
items.review_scope: Personally reread cited official fulltext paragraphs, verified cached bytes, and bound conservative bilingual summaries to those passages. Reused saved identity/date and primary/independent scope evidence. No whole-paper numerical recalculation or experimental rerun.

summary_source_claims.paragraph: LLM judges increasingly serve as quality gates for code changes that have no test oracle, but a judge prompt must be calibrated for its task and recalibrated as the system it judges evolves, while hand labels for the calibration are resource intensive and go stale. Development workflows emit outcome labels for free (tests pass or fail, changes land or are abandoned), but these labels are noisy. We present AutoRefine, a loop that rewrites a deployable judge’s prompt to reproduce outcome labels, with an informed teacher that sees the judge’s input plus the outcome, explains each label it keeps, and abstains when the outcome cannot be explained from what the judge sees. On a held-out dataset with an execution oracle, calibration raised chance-corrected agreement (Scott’s π \pi ) from 0.36 to 0.60. On a deployed agent’s outcome labels, with 25% flipped at random to introduce noise, the teacher set aside flipped fail labels at more than twice the rate of genuine ones, cutting overall label noise from 25% to 20%. Recalibrating that agent’s judge using AutoRefine raised its agreement with merge/abandon outcomes on 17 independently held-out diffs from the current workflow ( π \pi 0.16 to 0.51); on 16 diffs from older workflows, the previous judge stayed ahead, illustrating the need for recalibration as the agent evolves. By abstaining, the teacher not only removes noisy labels but also flags changes whose outcome the judge’s input cannot explain, telling a team when a judge needs better inputs rather than a better prompt.

The loop (Fig. 1 ) is an iterative optimizer over the judge’s prompt. The prompt plays the role of the parameters, agreement with the labels on the training split is the objective, disagreement analysis supplies the update direction, and a validation split decides when to stop. Each iteration runs the current prompt on the training split and scores its verdicts with Scott’s π \pi [ 4 ] , which corrects raw agreement for the agreement expected by chance from the pooled verdict and label distribution, so a judge that always predicts the majority class scores at or below zero ( − 0.08 -0.08 on our oracle test split). For every disagreement, an LLM (Claude Opus 4.7 in our runs) reads the judge’s verdict and reasoning next to the label and any teacher justification and proposes edits. The edits must be balanced, so every new reason to fail is paired with a reason to pass, which keeps the judge from drifting toward rejecting everything. A second call applies the edits under a length cap. For rubric judges, which emit a weighted score, the decision threshold is chosen on the training split. A separate validation split, never curated, selects the final prompt; the loop stops at a target agreement, when no disagreements remain, or at a maximum number of iterations (five in our runs, on training splits of 125 to 127 diffs). The agent’s patches are recorded once and replayed, so calibration never reruns the agent under test.

summary_override.summary_zh: AutoRefine 利用代码工作流中的合并、放弃等噪声标签，分析 judge 与标签的不一致，并反复改写可部署的质量评审提示。教师模型可以解释或弃权，候选提示由独立验证集选择。更新对象是评审组件的提示；实验重放已保存补丁，没有重新运行被评 Agent，因此不能将评审结果改善直接写成编码任务成功率提高。
summary_override.summary_en: AutoRefine uses noisy workflow labels, such as merge and abandonment outcomes, to analyze judge-label mismatches and iteratively revise a deployable code-quality review prompt. A teacher may explain a mismatch or abstain, and a separate validation set selects the prompt. The updated artifact is the review component. Experiments replay saved patches without rerunning the agent under test, so better judging does not directly establish improved coding-task success.

items.title: On Agentic Manipulation Policies
items.review_scope: Personally reread cited official fulltext paragraphs, verified cached bytes, and bound conservative bilingual summaries to those passages. Reused saved identity/date and primary/independent scope evidence. No whole-paper numerical recalculation or experimental rerun.

summary_source_claims.paragraph: In both the few-shot and the continual settings, the agent keeps whatever it finds useful in a persistent memory ℳ \mathcal{M} , a folder that it reads at the start of every episode. We impose no format on ℳ \mathcal{M} , so it may hold notes, code, or data in any form. Typically, the agent decides to keep a Markdown file of notes (strategies that succeeded or failed, pitfalls and observations, useful constants and parameters) and a Python library of code it found useful. Later episodes can read the notes and import and call the Python code. We refer to the harness augmented by the persistent memory ℳ \mathcal{M} as AMP1+.

In the few-shot setting, we let the agent learn a task by practicing it on several layouts until the agent judges that it can reliably succeed or reaches its practice budget. Each practice episode presents a new layout. The only feedback the agent receives is the benchmark’s official binary reward for each episode. This requires no expert demonstrations, no additional model training, and no reward shaping.

Our approach to learning from experience is gradient-free: the agent revises its memory and code, while the model weights remain fixed. This differs structurally from gradient-based approaches to few-shot learning [ 45 ] and continual learning [ 46 , 47 ] , which adapt neural network weights to new experience. Learning without weight updates has precedents in agents that retain verbal reflections [ 48 , 49 ] or accumulate executable skills [ 50 ] . In robotics, ASPIRE retains validated repair knowledge [ 36 ] , RoboSkill consolidates execution records into reusable guidance and code [ 51 ] , and RAX builds autonomous control programs and a persistent skill library through exploration [ 29 ] . ENPIRE automates policy improvement on physical robots, including both program refinement and gradient-based policy training [ 52 ] . We study gradient-free few-shot and continual learning with the generalist model continuing to reason and command the manipulator during execution, measuring both improvement on practiced tasks and transfer and retention across tasks.

In the continual setting, we test whether the agent can accumulate useful knowledge over its lifetime, applying lessons from earlier tasks to later ones. In this setting, the agent tackles an episode of each of the 42 RoboDojo tasks in random order. A persistent memory store ℳ \mathcal{M} is carried across tasks and the agent is instructed to keep only general lessons that may help with any task in the given robot embodiment.

What AMP1+ writes into its memory explains these results. From the earliest episodes, it records embodiment-specific knowledge, such as the robot’s coordinate frames, its physical limits, and how to work around the lack of depth sensing and camera calibration. It also writes code for basic manipulation primitives, such as grasping and placing. Because these findings apply to every task, they benefit later episodes as well.

summary_override.summary_zh: AMP 的代码学习分支让操控 Agent 在模型权重固定时，根据任务成功反馈修订持久存储中的代码与记忆。可复用的 Python 操控函数能被后续任务导入调用，形成跨任务保留的可执行组件。这里纳入的是该代码更新分支；仅保存文字经验或使用固定框架，不足以据此认定 Harness 演化，也不能扩大为任意真实机器人上的泛化结论。
summary_override.summary_en: The code-learning branch of AMP lets a manipulation agent revise code and memory in persistent storage using task-success feedback while model weights stay fixed. Reusable Python manipulation functions can be imported by later tasks, providing executable components that persist across tasks. Inclusion is limited to this code-update branch; storing textual experience or using a fixed framework alone does not establish Harness evolution, nor do these results establish generality across arbitrary real robots.

items.title: Rethinking Agent Trajectory Compression: A Workflow-Aware Perspective
items.review_scope: Personally reread cited official fulltext paragraphs, verified cached bytes, and bound conservative bilingual summaries to those passages. Reused saved identity/date and primary/independent scope evidence. No whole-paper numerical recalculation or experimental rerun.

summary_source_claims.paragraph: Only trajectories that pass task-level verification are inserted into the history store. A history entry contains the canonical fragment, verification metadata, and the field-level policies observed in that trajectory. It does not contain concrete executable actions or external side effects.

Development trajectories are collected from the development split using initial compression policy and library initialization. At each compression checkpoint u u in trajectory τ \tau , we record the observable fragment F τ , u F_{\tau,u} , its canonical field correspondence, and the policy ρ t ​ ( f ) \rho_{t}(f) actually applied after representation validation and fallback. The fragment and policy record therefore describe the state available at that checkpoint. After task-level verification confirms success, these records are admitted to the history library and aligned to canonical fields.

SemSim \operatorname{SemSim} is the cosine similarity between normalized semantic descriptions of eligible fragments, and the maximum selects the highest-scoring compatible match. The semantic description captures workflow meaning for retrieval, while the canonical structure determines whether the proposed field correspondence is admissible. The selected entry contributes its field-level policy proposal ρ ^ t ​ ( f ) \widehat{\rho}_{t}(f) ; concrete artifact values and executable actions are supplied by the current trajectory. Historical policies are transferred only through validated field correspondences. Fields without an admissible correspondence receive no historical retention constraint. If no compatible candidate passes the acceptance threshold, the decision uses online requirements alone.

After receiving the compressed context, the agent chooses its next action and executes the corresponding tool. The resulting observation updates the graph and outstanding obligations for the next decision. A completed trajectory can contribute to the history store only after task-level verification confirms success, while unverified executions do not become successful policy precedents.

Fusion selects a representation that satisfies both the current dependency requirement and the retrieved historical policy. Under the preservation order, this is expressed as Fuse ⁡ ( a , b ) = max ≺ ⁡ ( a , b ) \operatorname{Fuse}(a,b)=\max_{\prec}(a,b) . SUMMARY and POINTER provide different capabilities: the former exposes bounded semantic information, while the latter supports access to an external artifact. When both capabilities are required and neither representation alone is sufficient, the conservative choice is EXACT. If the history is empty or no compatible fragment is found, the final policy reduces to d t ​ ( f ) d_{t}(f) . Historical experience therefore supplies an additional retention constraint; it does not relax a requirement established by the current workflow. Specific details can be found in Appendix A .

The selected policies are applied to the model-visible context while the original trajectory and runtime artifacts remain available. An exact field is exposed unchanged, a summary retains the required semantic content, a pointer identifies an externally recoverable object, and a dropped field is omitted from the visible representation. Pointer use requires a valid reference to the intended artifact, and uncertain recovery must fall back to exact retention. The same conservative principle applies when a reduced representation cannot be shown to satisfy the registered requirements. These conditions bound the preservation claim to the dependencies and schemas represented by the system.

Matching and fusion remain fixed, so this is not evidence of self-rewriting compression source code or merely accumulating general experience content.

items.title: When Feedback Becomes a Backdoor: Tracing Backdoor Skill Formation in Text-Space Skill Optimization
items.review_scope: Personally reread cited official fulltext paragraphs, verified cached bytes, and bound conservative bilingual summaries to those passages. Reused saved identity/date and primary/independent scope evidence. No whole-paper numerical recalculation or experimental rerun.

summary_source_claims.paragraph: Reference answers are a supervision channel in text-space Skill optimization, which produces reusable text artifacts called Skills that guide future agent behavior. Poisoning those answers can induce a persistent trigger-conditioned rule without giving the attacker access to the model, optimizer, or Skill file. We study this reference-feedback poisoning in SkillOpt by tracing an attacker-supplied trigger–payload mapping from reflection to held-out activation. In SearchQA, where the payload replaces a short answer, the natural attack retains an exact rule in all three seeds; each final Skill emits the payload on 200/200 triggered questions and 0/200 clean questions. In seed 42, removing the rule eliminates activation, and an in-run comparison shows similar clean accuracy to benign SkillOpt (169/200 versus 171/200). In SpreadsheetBench, where the payload requires an additional workbook edit, no natural run retains an exact rule across three seeds. Diagnostic interventions locate two successive bottlenecks: the Analyst abstracts away required literals, and, once literal preservation is enabled, edit-budget ranking can remove exact edits before candidate construction. Poisoned references can therefore create persistent backdoors, but exposure alone does not ensure that the induced rule is formed, selected, and retained.

We show a complete natural attack chain across repeated runs in a short-answer setting, including selective held-out activation and paired rule deletion. In a structured, tool-mediated setting where the natural chain stops before exact-rule retention, we use targeted diagnostics to locate successive formation and ranking bottlenecks.

Limitations. Natural end-to-end success covers one SearchQA mapping across three seeds. We audited the endpoints of the other trigger constructions across seeds 42–44 (Table 12 ). Each validation-poison level was examined in one trajectory. The two task settings use task-specific SkillOpt configurations, including different update counts and slow-update settings. Their outcomes should therefore be interpreted as complementary case studies, not as a controlled comparison that isolates task modality as the cause of success or failure. The benign comparison is available only for seed 42, and TBA only for SpreadsheetBench. Most support-grid cells also use seed 42. Results come from one optimizer and one closed model; broader models, tasks, and defenses remain untested. Prompt and budget interventions are diagnostics, and SpreadsheetBench activation/deletion relies on one 40-source lineage.

items.title: Flex-RSI: Benchmarking Recursive Self-Improvement of Frontier Agents
items.review_scope: Personally reread cited official fulltext paragraphs, verified cached bytes, and bound conservative bilingual summaries to those passages. Reused saved identity/date and primary/independent scope evidence. No whole-paper numerical recalculation or experimental rerun.

summary_source_claims.paragraph: Each task provides the agent with a starter solution, compute resources, a budget, and data partitioned into three disjoint splits. The development split , including its labels, is available to the agent for experimentation and evaluation. The validation split is withheld from the agent and determines which candidate solutions are retained. The test split is likewise withheld and is used only once, after the run terminates, to evaluate the final solution. The objective of the agent is to maximize the test score of its final solution within the budget.

A harness is the program that mediates between a language model and a task. Through its prompts, tools, control loop, and memory, it determines the context presented to the model and the actions available to it. Since the harness consists of code and text, the agent can modify it in the same manner as any other program, while the model weights remain fixed. In Flex-RSI, the harness H = ( E , I ) H=(E,I) comprises two components that query the same model. The executor E E operates on the task solution: it modifies the solution, conducts experiments, and evaluates the results on the development split. The improver I I operates on the harness: it analyses the executor’s trajectories and results, diagnoses failures, and revises the prompts, tools, and workflow of the executor as well as its own instructions and accumulated lessons.
Finally, the improver examines the records τ 1 : t \tau_{1:t} of all rounds so far, which comprise the executor’s trajectories, experiments, and scores, and produces the harness for the next round:

Equation 3 makes the recursion explicit: the improver is both the operator that produces the next harness and one of its arguments, so that a modification of I I changes how all subsequent modifications are made. The decomposition also separates the two kinds of improvement. A change to the solution takes effect only after it has been confirmed on data unseen by the agent ( Equation 2 ), whereas a change to the harness is reflected in the candidates of subsequent rounds ( Equation 1 ).

All runs start from the same general-purpose harness H 0 H_{0} , which contains no task- or model-specific components. The evaluator S S , the data splits, and the accounting of the budget are fixed and cannot be modified by the agent. Differences between runs can therefore be attributed to the agents themselves, and runs of different models on the same task are directly comparable.

Each model is run once on each task it is evaluated on; where a run was repeated, the latest run is reported. RoboDojo and RoboCasa are suites of 10 and 8 robot tasks, each run separately for 10 rounds and aggregated into one suite score. A run’s result is the test score of its final solution on the task’s primary metric, on a 0–100 scale. Because the metrics differ across tasks, models are compared through ranks: on each task, a model scores the share of the other models evaluated on the task that it beats, from 0 (last) to 100 (first). Its score in an area is the mean over the tasks of the area it was run on, and its overall score is the mean of its five area scores. To measure self-improvement itself, we also report the validation score of the starter solution and the best validation score reached during the run. The main results cover the 20 tasks evaluated with at least six models; the four tasks evaluated with two models so far are reported in Table 12 .

Table 8 compares pairs of runs that differ only in whether the improver runs. In the run without the improver, labeled frozen harness in the table, the starting harness is never modified; in the run with it, labeled self-improving harness, the improver edits the executor and itself after every round, as in all other runs of this report. The test score with the improver is higher in six of the seven pairs, by 2.0 to 40.0 points; in the seventh, Claude Opus 5.5 on Turn On Sink Faucet reaches 80.0 in both runs, and its run without the improver reached the maximum validation score in round 8. The difference is largest where the unchanged starting harness makes little progress: DeepSeek-V4.1 Flash remains at 0.0 on Open Drawer without the improver and reaches 40.0 with it, and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next gains 20.0 on Turn On Sink Faucet and 38.3 on Active Search. On 3D Tracking, the executor alone already raises the two Qwen models from the 19.4 of the starter solution to validation scores of 48.9 and 63.4, and the improver adds 6.5 and 2.0 points on the test split. The runs without the improver also end after fewer rounds in six of the seven pairs.

summary_override.summary_zh: Flex-RSI 将任务解的改进与 Harness 改进分开：executor 修改解，improver 根据轨迹和结果改写 executor 及自身的提示、工具与工作流，后续轮次继续使用更新后的 Harness。模型权重、评估器和数据划分固定，最终解在隐藏测试集评分；论文另用冻结 Harness 配对运行检验 Harness 编辑的贡献。应归 Harness 专项评测，但各模型任务覆盖不齐、通常每格单次运行，不能据此夸大稳健性或跨任务迁移。
summary_override.summary_en: Flex-RSI separates solution improvement from harness improvement: an executor edits the task solution, while an improver uses trajectories and results to revise the executor and its own prompts, tools, and workflow for later rounds. Model weights, evaluators, and data splits stay fixed, and the final solution is evaluated on hidden test data. Paired frozen-harness runs study the contribution of harness editing. Uneven task coverage and generally single runs limit claims of robustness or cross-task transfer.

items.title: BOXBOX: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement for Long-Running Performance Optimization
items.review_scope: Personally reread cited official fulltext paragraphs, verified cached bytes, and bound conservative bilingual summaries to those passages. Reused saved identity/date and primary/independent scope evidence. No whole-paper numerical recalculation or experimental rerun.

summary_source_claims.paragraph: To address these limitations, we introduce BoxBox 1 1 1 Named after the F1 radio call “box, box,” requesting a pit stop for repairs and adjustments during the race. to support agent-triggered revision of the full executable harness through kernel-managed hot reloading. When requested, the kernel pauses task execution and launches an agent review session to diagnose difficulties from the trajectory and revise the harness. After validation, it resumes the task with preserved execution context under the revised harness, which governs both subsequent execution and future reviews, enabling recursive harness improvement. We evaluate BoxBox on PerfRace against Frozen Harness, offline Harness Evolution and externally controlled Harness Scaling under matched task budgets, comparing best-so-far correct speedup and model cost. BoxBox achieves a Speedup ​ @ ​ 4 ​ h \mathrm{Speedup@}4\mathrm{h} of 1.70 × 1.70\times , compared with 1.44 × 1.44\times for Frozen Harness, 1.28 × 1.28\times for Harness Evolution, and 1.54 × 1.54\times for Harness Scaling.

BoxBox treats the harness as a task-specific implementation, allowing a revision to be tailored to the requirements of the ongoing task. To support such adaptations, BoxBox exposes the full executable harness, allowing the agent to translate task-specific needs into direct changes to tools, control flow, and state management. Let ℋ \mathcal{H} denote the set of harness implementations compatible with the execution interface. Methods with predefined editable components restrict candidate revisions to a subset ℋ bounded ⊆ ℋ \mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{bounded}}\subseteq\mathcal{H} ( Zhang et al., 2026b ; Lin et al., 2026 ; Park et al., 2026 ) , whereas BoxBox allows revisions H k ′ ∈ ℋ H^{\prime}_{k}\in\mathcal{H} .

Specifically, we register boxbox() as a tool that yields control to the kernel, with boxbox() ∈ 𝒜 ⁡ ( H k ) \texttt{boxbox()}\in\mathcal{A}(H_{k}) . When the agent invokes boxbox() , the kernel suspends task execution and preserves the agent’s execution context, including the accumulated trajectory, terminal session, and workspace state. It then launches a review session for the agent to examine the trajectory, revise the harness as needed, and commit any changes. After the review session concludes, the kernel validates any new commits, loads the revised runtime on success, and otherwise retains the current runtime. During activation, the kernel transfers the preserved execution context to the new runtime and reattaches the existing terminal session. On successful activation, H k + 1 = H k ′ H_{k+1}=H^{\prime}_{k} , and subsequent interactions follow Eqn. 1 . Finally, the kernel returns control to the agent, allowing it to resume the ongoing task.

Diagnosis. The agent examines the trajectory for execution failures, repeated work, and successful patterns that could be automated or reused. It uses these observations to identify limitations of the current harness, such as missing capabilities or costly tool interactions.

Baselines. We compare BoxBox with three baselines: Frozen Harness ( Frozen ) retains the initial harness throughout task execution. Harness Evolution ( HE ) optimizes the harness offline on training tasks and selects it by validation performance, then holds it fixed during test-task execution. Harness Scaling ( HS ) uses an external controller to revise the harness between attempts on the same task, using feedback from each completed attempt. Both HE and HS are adapted from Wang et al. (2026b) . Following Meta-Harness ( Lee et al., 2026 ) , all methods start from the same initial harness H 0 H_{0} , Terminus-KIRA ( KRAFTON AI and Ludo Robotics, 2026 ) , a simple terminal-based harness that executes shell commands and returns their outputs to the model.

Evaluation protocol. We split the 100 PerfRace tasks into 40 training and 10 validation tasks for HE , and 50 held-out test tasks for evaluating all methods. Both task execution and harness optimization are performed using GPT-5.6 Luna with high reasoning effort. Each method is evaluated with three independent runs per test task, each sharing a four-hour budget ( B = 4 ​ h B=4\mathrm{h} ) across task execution, harness optimization, and evaluation. Detailed configurations are provided in Appendix A .

Offline harness optimization does not reliably improve performance. HE reaches 1.281 × 1.281\times at four hours, below Frozen (Table 1 ). HE struggles to identify consistently effective harness revisions during training, while the revisions selected through validation show limited generalization to long-running test tasks. Appendix A.2 provides detailed results and failure analysis. HE costs an average of $24.56 per test run. Including offline training and validation costs, shared across the 150 test runs, brings this average to at least $33.73. This additional offline expenditure does not translate into better test performance or greater cost efficiency than Frozen .

summary_override.summary_zh: BOXBOX 让 Agent 在长时任务中根据执行困难主动复审并改写自己的可执行 Harness。kernel 验证改动后保留上下文、热加载新运行时，后续执行和复审继续使用新版。PerfRace 上与固定 Harness、离线 Harness Evolution 和外部控制的 Harness Scaling 比较，使用相同任务时间预算；这是任务内跨轮 Harness 演化证据，独立跨任务迁移仍为 unknown，不能把时间预算相同写成费用完全相同。
summary_override.summary_en: BOXBOX lets an agent request reviews and rewrite its executable harness in response to difficulties during a long-running task. A kernel validates the changes and hot-reloads the runtime while preserving execution context; the revised harness governs later execution and reviews. PerfRace comparisons use matched task-time budgets against frozen, offline-evolved, and externally controlled harness baselines. This supports within-task inheritance across improvement rounds; independent cross-task transfer remains unknown and equal time does not imply equal dollar cost.
